title: Inflation rate jumps to 4.9% as Australia’s cost-of-living crisis intensifies
summary: Figure up from 4.3% annual rate in September and nearly double Reserve Bank’s official target of 2.5%

blocks.text: Surging fuel costs and the end of electricity rebates have helped drive inflation to 4.9% in the year to October, from 4.3%, as cost-of-living pressures peak in the lead-up to Christmas.
Alongside a 6.3% increase in fuel costs last month, the latest figures from the Australian Bureau of Statistics showed electricity prices were 25% higher than a year earlier.
The latest consumer price report comes two days after Jim Chalmers, the treasurer, stood up in parliament to warn Australians that economic conditions would get worse before they got better.
Chalmers in a statement said “this inflation challenge is the primary influence on the budget update we will finalise in the coming weeks and release in December”.

“We will respond with substantial savings and we have already announced additional cost of living help this week,” he said, referring to Monday’s announcement that the $25 price cap on PBS medicines would be extended to the end of the decade.
Stephen Smith, a partner at Deloitte Access Economics, said the inflation numbers “underscore the difficult balance facing the federal government”.
“The treasurer must attempt to hand down a budget update that cuts enough to take some pressure off inflation, but avoids cruelling an economy on the cusp of a downturn,” Smith said.

Rachael McCririck, the ABS head of price statistics, said the huge increase in power bills reflected the end of government subsidies, “which reduced household electricity costs last year but are no longer in place”.
McCririck said removing the impact of these “temporary shocks” provided a better idea of underlying price pressures in the economy.
But even here, the news was worse than expected. The Reserve Bank’s preferred trimmed mean measure of inflation – which takes out the most volatile prices – lifted to 3.8%.
Economists had expected it to stay at 3.6%.
Amid rising fears of a recession, financial markets before the release of the latest worse-than-expected inflation data had been pricing in an RBA rate cut by August.
Brendan Rynne, the chief economist at KPMG, said the RBA was “between a rock and a hard place”, with inflation and unemployment both accelerating to 4.9%.
Rynne said he did not expect a sixth interest rate hike at the central bank’s final board meeting of the year on 7-8 December.
“Today’s inflation jump is not the kind of spike the RBA will be wanting to see, but it’s still unlikely to result in a further rate rise this year,” he said.
“Instead, we expect they’ll hold until February to see how the numbers look between now and then.”
Analysts are hopeful that inflation will ease through 2027 to be back below 3% in 12 months’ time, as the shocks of this year ebb away.
